1.pericope_label: The eighth day: the offerings appointed and the glory promised

schools.summary: Gill weighs the Jewish datings of the eighth day and settles with Aben Ezra for the eighth of Nisan, the day after the anointing of Aaron and his sons. Calvin sets out the architecture of the whole chapter before entering it: the earlier part shows how Aaron, after seven days' initiation, began the work entrusted to him, the second how the sacrifices were approved by a divine miracle that ratified the priesthood God had instituted. He also stops on something easy to pass over, that Moses, never appointed priest by any solemn rite, was the one who sanctified the others, so that the authority and efficacy of the outward sign should be seen to rest in God alone. On the promise of the appearing he holds that though Moses seems to address the whole people he speaks especially to Aaron's sons, for whom it was no common aid to faith that their office should be sealed by God himself.

Henry finds the timing instructive. The priests had not one day's respite to receive the compliments of their friends but were employed the very next day, a sign they were not ordained to be idle; he that desires the office of a bishop desires a good work, which must be looked at more than the honour and the benefit, and God's spiritual priests have constant work cut out for them. On the calf he reports the Jewish writers' suggestion that it was chosen to remind Aaron of his sin in making the golden calf, by which he had rendered himself for ever unworthy of the priesthood and on which he had reason to reflect with sorrow in all his atonements. And he presses the pastoral consequence of Aaron sacrificing for himself first: those who have care of other souls must look to their own first, since we cannot expect acceptance in prayer for others while unreconciled ourselves, a charity that must begin at home though it must not end there.

Clarke supports the symbolism of the eighth day from Ainsworth with a run of parallels, circumcision, young beasts, those unclean by leprosy, all imperfect for seven days and perfected on the eighth. On the calf he observes that no formal atonement for the golden calf had yet been made, which is what makes the traditional explanation probable. He also notices a difficulty in the animal named for the people, since the law elsewhere requires a young bullock for the sin of the congregation and a kid for a ruler's, and suspects this offering may have been meant for the elders themselves, though he allows the commoner solution that the earlier law was for a particular sin and this for sin in general. Wesley repeats the golden-calf explanation almost word for word, gives the same solution to Clarke's difficulty, and notes that the Hebrew of the promise says the Lord hath appeared, speaking of a thing to come as though it were past, which is frequent in scripture and gives the more assurance.

Ellicott puts the eighth day most neatly: as newly-born children remain seven days unclean and enter the covenant privileges of the congregation on the eighth, so the newly-created priests, after a purging of seven days, began their sacred duties on that symbolical day. He identifies the company exactly, the elders summoned here being the same representatives who attested the consecration, now called to witness the priests entering on their active duties, and later called the children of Israel because they act for the people, which is why the Greek version renders the phrase elders in that place too. On the calf he makes the traditional reading evidential rather than merely edifying: this is the only instance in which a calf is appointed for a sin offering, the offerer commanded to bring it is Aaron, and the reading is so old that the ancient Chaldee version already expresses it. He suggests that Aaron sacrificed for himself first to expiate whatever pride he might have fostered at being so distinguished.

the calf that recalled the golden calf

7.pericope_label: Aaron's own sin offering and burnt offering

schools.summary: Gill, like Ellicott, stops on Aaron's waiting to be told, not approaching the altar until Moses called him. Calvin takes the deeper argument furthest. The apostle justly infers from a high priest who must atone for himself that the legal priesthood was weak and merely typical, for none can be a true peace-maker but one who, relying on his own perfect innocence, presents himself before God to obtain pardon for others, and who, being pure from every blemish, requires no expiation for himself. The rite that qualified Aaron is thus the same rite that exposed the limits of his office.

Henry watches what Aaron actually did and finds two things in it. He slew the victim with his own hands, doing the work of the inferior priests, since great as he was he must think nothing below him that he could do for God's honour; and as Moses had shown him how to do it, so he showed his sons, that being the best way of teaching and the way parents should instruct their children. Henry also notes that all this was done besides the burnt sacrifice of the morning, and draws from it that our accustomed devotions, morning and evening, alone and in our families, must not be omitted on any pretence: whatever is added, these must not be diminished. On what fire consumed Aaron's offerings he canvasses three views and then proposes a fourth of his own, that the fire from the Lord fastened on what was already there and put out the fire Aaron had kindled, as a greater fire puts out a less, consuming suddenly what the lesser would have consumed slowly.

Clarke states the inference briefly, that the high priest's needing to atone for himself first showed the imperfection of the Levitical law. Wesley gives it a pastoral edge: first for thyself, otherwise thou art unfit to do it for the people, God teaching us both the deficiency of that priesthood and how needful it is that ministers stand in his favour themselves if their ministrations are to be acceptable and profitable. On the blood Wesley draws the sharpest distinction of the three who explain it, that in the earlier law the priest is supposed complete in his office whereas here he is but entering it, and must sanctify himself at the brazen altar before he can be admitted where the altar of incense stands. He holds the fire used to have been ordinary fire, adds that it was lawful because done at the command of Moses, and observes that nothing is expressly said to be consumed by the heavenly fire except the burnt offering with its fat.

Ellicott draws the conclusion from Aaron's waiting: though now the installed high priest, he did not approach the altar till Moses called him, showing the representatives of the people that he had not taken the honour to himself but held it by the call of God through Moses, which is the apostle's own point. He explains, with Wesley, why the blood never entered the holy place, Aaron simply putting some on the horns of the brazen altar as Moses had at the consecration, because though high priest he had no access to the sanctuary until this sacrifice qualified him; and he takes the fire to have been ordinary, the miraculous fire not issuing until the people's burnt offering was made. Keil supplies the order of the three offerings and the reason for it, an explanation that governs the rest of the chapter: the sin offering first, removing the estrangement from a holy God which sin had caused and clearing the hindrances to approach; the burnt offering next, as the expression of the expiated person's complete surrender; the peace offering last, at once thanksgiving for mercy received and a seal of covenant fellowship in the sacrificial meal.

themes: no man taketh this honour unto himself
the priest who must first be atoned for

14.pericope_label: The people's offerings, the daily sacrifice, and the priestly blessing

schools.summary: Gill explains what the peace offerings were for, that the people might feast and be glad that atonement had been made for their sins and their gifts accepted of God, and he sets down the rabbinic prescriptions for the posture of blessing in some detail, the hands raised to the shoulders in the provinces and above the head in the sanctuary, the fingers parted so as to leave five spaces, the palms turned toward the earth. Calvin states most fully what the gesture meant. It was a kind of application of the sacrifice, so that the people might know God was reconciled to them through the priest as their mediator and surety, and when by lifting up their hands the priests testified of God's fatherly favour their commission was ratified and made efficacious. He finds a memorable instance in the chronicler, where the priests and Levites blessed the people and their prayer came up to God's holy dwelling place, and sees the fulfilment of the type in Christ, who is not only the source and cause of blessing but publishes it by the gospel with effect.

Wesley states in a line the principle behind the morning sacrifice being offered first: God will not have his ordinary and stated service swallowed up by the extraordinary. He reads the posture of blessing as signifying both whence Aaron expected the blessing and his hearty desire of it for the people, and insists that blessing was an act of his priestly office no less than sacrificing. Clarke supplies the form of words from Numbers and then states the purpose of the whole day's work: the sacrifices were made not to confer any obligation on God, but to make atonement for sin and to engage him to dwell among his worshippers and influence them.

Ellicott follows the ritual detail by detail. On the washing and burning he observes that no special fire was to be kindled for the burnt offering, which was laid on top of the sin offering already burning; at the turn to the people's sacrifices he marks the transition exactly, that being reconciled to God by the atoning sacrifice offered for his own share in the sin, Aaron was now qualified to offer the sin offering of the people and conducted its ritual just as he had conducted his own. He gives the practical shape of the daily offering too, that Aaron began his priestly functions with the daily morning sacrifice, which took precedence of all others and was never superseded by additional ones. On the blessing he reports the ancient practice as a living one, the descendants of Aaron pronouncing this benediction upon the congregation in the synagogue to this day, obliged in accordance with the words here to turn their faces to the people, and joining thumbs and forefingers so as to produce a triple division of the hand. Keil summarises the remaining stages, the burnt offering presented in the prescribed manner, the meat offering, the peace offerings of bullock and ram with the blood sprinkled round about, and the breasts and right shoulder waved before the Lord.

debates.question: What did the lifting up of the priest's hands signify?

positions.position: an application of the sacrifice, by which the priests' commission to declare God reconciled was ratified and made efficacious
whence Aaron expected the blessing, and his hearty desire of it for the people

outliers.note: reports the Aaronic benediction not as an antiquity but as a rite still performed in the synagogue, down to the position of the hands and the turning of the face toward the people

themes: the daily sacrifice not swallowed up by the extraordinary
the lifting up of the priest’s hands
blessing as an act of the priestly office

23.pericope_label: Moses and Aaron go in, and the glory appears

schools.summary: Gill offers the reasons tradition gives for the entry, Jarchi's that Moses went in to teach Aaron the business of the incense, and the Targum's that he went in to pray for the people and for the appearance that had been promised them, with Aben Ezra's addition that fire might descend on the sacrifices as a token of acceptance. Calvin notices the change of subject in the verse, that what was said of Aaron alone in the previous verse is now ascribed to Moses also, and for a different reason, since though Moses was God's prophet, Aaron in right of his office was the only mediator. He also allows the clause about the glory to be read either as a statement complete in itself or as running straight on into what follows, in which case the account of the consuming of the sacrifice is its exposition, and God appeared precisely when he sent forth the fire.

Henry draws the inference the whole day has been building toward. The glory appeared not while the sacrifices were in offering but when the priests prayed, and it was when Moses and Aaron concurred in praying that the people had what they had been waiting for; God's manifestations of himself, of his glory and grace, are commonly given in answer to prayer, as when Christ was praying and the heavens were opened. What the appearance was he will not say, only that it carried its own evidence along with it. His figure for it is the one that stays: the glory which had filled the tabernacle now showed itself at the door to those who attended there, as a prince shows himself to the expecting crowd, to gratify them; and those who diligently attend upon God in the way he has appointed shall have such a sight of his glory as shall be abundantly to their satisfaction.

Clarke supposes that Moses accompanied Aaron into the tabernacle to show him how to offer the incense, prepare the lamps and the perfume, and adjust the shewbread. Wesley says the same and then defines the verb that follows: to bless is to pray to God for his blessing upon them, and here particularly for his gracious acceptance of these and all succeeding sacrifices and for his signification of it by some extraordinary token, which is exactly what followed. He takes the glory to have been either a miraculous brightness shining from the cloudy pillar or else a glorious and visible discovery of God's gracious presence and acceptance of the present service.

Ellicott gives the fullest account of the errand. The sacrifices being ended, there still remained the burning of the incense on the golden altar within, so Aaron, conducted by Moses, left the court where the altar of burnt offering stood and went into the holy place; and Moses, having already delivered to him the charge of everything connected with the sacrifices in the court, now committed to him the care of the things within the sanctuary as well, showing him how to offer the incense, how to arrange the shewbread, how to light and trim the lamps. He preserves the words tradition gives the blessing, from the Chaldee version of the Pentateuch, that the word of the Lord accept your sacrifice with favour and remit and pardon your sins, and takes the glory for the cloudy pillar in a more luminous appearance, visible in greater effulgence to all the people who witnessed the installation. Keil dissents from both halves of the usual account: not to offer incense, which would undoubtedly have been mentioned, nor yet for the special purpose of praying for the manifestation of the glory, but to introduce Aaron into the sanctuary in which he was henceforth to serve the Lord and to present him to the Lord, though there can be no doubt that they prayed there for the right discharge of the office entrusted to them.

schools.summary: Gill canvasses both of the open questions. On whence the fire came he allows either heaven or the holy of holies, where the symbol of the divine presence was and Jehovah had now taken up his residence. On what it consumed he sets two incompatible accounts side by side: Aben Ezra's, that the burnt offering means Aaron's and the people's and the daily sacrifice together, since the text has said the morning burnt offering was besides these, with the fat of the calf and ram of Aaron and of the goat and ox and ram of the people, which though laid on the altar as each was offered were on this view not burnt until now; and Bishop Patrick's, that the offering of all these sacrifices had taken up the whole day from the morning sacrifice until the evening, that what was consumed here was the evening burnt offering, and that all the rest had been burnt with common fire and this alone with fire from the Lord.

Clarke breaks the people's response into three: the miracle was done in such a way as gave them the fullest conviction of its reality; they exulted in the thought that the God of almighty power had taken up his abode among them; and they prostrated themselves, intimating the deep sense they had of his goodness, of their own unworthiness, and of the obligation they were under to live in obedience to his will. He follows the fire down the history, carefully preserved among the Israelites till the time of Solomon, when it was renewed, and continued among them until the Babylonish captivity, and reads it as the emblem of the Holy Spirit: as no sacrifice was acceptable that had not been seasoned by this fire, so no soul can offer acceptably but through the influences of the Divine Spirit; and if we hope to see him as he is, we must resemble him. Wesley locates the fire as from the place where God was in a special manner present, either from heaven or from the holy of holies, notes that it was to be carefully kept and never suffered to lapse and was therefore carried in a peculiar vessel on their journeys, and reads it forward in a sentence: thus the Spirit descended in fire upon the apostles, so ratifying their commission as this ratified that of the priests, and the descent of this holy fire into our souls, to kindle in them devout affections and such a holy zeal as burns up all unholiness, is a certain token of God's gracious acceptance.

Ellicott catches what made the sight unmistakable: the victims that ordinarily continued smouldering on the altar all the day and all the night were consumed suddenly, in the people's sight, by flashes of fire sent out from the luminous cloud. He lists the later occasions on which God testified his acceptance by the same token, the offering of Gideon, Elijah's on Carmel, and Solomon's at the dedication of the Temple, and reports the tradition that the fire which thus issued from the immediate presence of God continued to be nourished on the altar with fuel especially provided by the congregation, and so constituted the perpetual fire. In the people's shout he hears the words the chronicler records at the dedication, when the sons of Israel saw how the fire came down and the glory of the Lord shone upon the house, and bowed themselves with their faces to the ground and praised the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever.

outliers.note: reports two irreconcilable accounts of what the fire consumed without choosing between them — Aben Ezra's, that it took all the day's burnt offerings and fat at once, and Bishop Patrick's, that it took only the evening sacrifice, the rest having been burnt with common fire

themes: the perpetual fire and its later history
the shout and the falling on their faces
